headline: Massachusetts water board approves $80 million for wastewater, PFAS and stormwater projects
dek: The latest Clean Water Trust package directs low-interest financing and grants to Gloucester, Provincetown, Manchester-by-the-Sea, Revere, Nantucket and Harwich.
body: Massachusetts’ Clean Water Trust board approved $80,141,116 in new grants and low-interest loans on Oct. 7, directing fresh financing toward wastewater treatment, sewer expansion, drinking-water protection and utility cybersecurity projects in communities across the state. The award list reaches from Gloucester and Provincetown to Manchester-by-the-Sea, Revere, Nantucket and Harwich. The [Massachusetts Clean Water Trust announcement](https://www.mass.gov/news/clean-water-trust-approves-801-million-in-new-grants-and-loans-at-its-october-meeting) identifies the package as a mix of State Revolving Fund loans and smaller targeted grants, rather than a single statewide construction program.

The largest commitment is a $50 million loan to Gloucester for secondary treatment and facility upgrades at the city’s Water Pollution Control Facility. The loan carries a 1.5% interest rate. Gloucester says on its [project funding page](https://gloucester-ma.gov/1573/Funding) that the work is being financed primarily through the Massachusetts Clean Water State Revolving Fund, with the treatment upgrades tied to the facility’s long-term compliance and water-quality obligations. The Trust’s [Oct. 7 board materials](https://www.mass.gov/doc/board-materials-1072026/download) describe replacement of aged systems and the addition of secondary treatment in accordance with the city’s federal discharge permit and an Environmental Protection Agency consent decree.

Provincetown is slated to receive a $13,901,116 loan at 1.5% for Phase 6B of its sewer collection-system expansion. The board materials say the phase would extend service into nine currently unsewered subareas and serve 513 properties. That award follows the town’s announcement that it had received more than $2 million in separate state grants for infrastructure, planning and public safety, including a MassWorks award for sewer service near Nelson Avenue. Together, the decisions show how Provincetown is assembling several funding sources for a townwide sewer buildout while connecting infrastructure planning to future housing capacity.

Manchester-by-the-Sea’s $13.44 million, 2% drinking-water loan is aimed at PFAS treatment at the Lincoln Street Well. According to the board materials, the well has an approved withdrawal rate of 0.38 million gallons per day and supplies about 40% of the town’s water. The planned process combines greensand pressure vessels for iron and manganese treatment with granular activated carbon for PFAS. The town’s [PFAS information page](https://manchester.ma.us/777/PFAS) says officials have been testing the Lincoln Street Well and Gravelly Pond under state and federal requirements since 2021; the new award finances a treatment project, but it does not by itself establish a new contamination finding or change public-health guidance.

Revere’s awards address a different pressure: inflow and conveyance in a sewer system subject to a consent decree. The Trust approved two planning loans, worth $1.25 million and $500,000, for continued assessment and project planning. The board documents say the work includes evaluating inflow removal, the Waitt Park Pumping Station and Force Main project, and alternatives for reducing combined-sewer overflow risk. Revere also received a $250,000 Sewer Overflow and Stormwater Reuse Municipal Grant, making the city the only community in the package listed for both planning loans and a stormwater grant.

The remaining awards are smaller but touch different parts of municipal water management. Nantucket received a $750,000 loan at 2% through the Community Septic Management Program. Harwich received a $50,000 cybersecurity improvement grant for drinking-water infrastructure. The Trust says its programs are run with the Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection through state revolving funds, which operate as an environmental infrastructure bank supported by the Commonwealth and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.

For residents, the immediate news is a financing commitment, not a promise that every project will be built on the same timetable. Each borrower still has to move through its own design, permitting, contracting and construction steps, and the board’s approval does not settle the final cost or schedule of local work. The state says the Trust has loaned roughly $10.4 billion since its creation in 1989 and estimates that 97% of Massachusetts residents have benefited from its assistance. The new round’s practical effect will be measured locally: in Gloucester’s treatment capacity, Provincetown’s sewered properties, Manchester-by-the-Sea’s drinking-water safeguards and Revere’s effort to control sewer and stormwater flows.
author: NorthEast News Desk
